content.text: Now phase 7 — the backfill Workflow, which needs nothing from Cloudflare to build against fixtures:

content.content:
Per-source modules behind **one shared fetch module** — retries, backoff,
bot-wall detection, and raw-before-parse discipline live there once. Each source
module declares the data surface it reads (hydration blob, client API, or
markup — in that order of preference), its own refresh clock, and an extractor
from raw payload to candidate utterances. Fields the extractor doesn't yet
understand are preserved in the raw record, not dropped.

Two drivers over the same modules:

- **The backfill** walks a source's archive in slices — a year of one archive is
  the working unit — as one Workflow run per slice. A slice that fails retries
  without touching its neighbours, and the window is finite, so the job has an
  end.
- **The cron** covers the moving edge, on each source's own clock. A transcript
  archive and a press feed do not move at the same speed, and running everything
  on the fastest one re-learns a static document thousands of times.

Cloudflare egress comes from datacenter IPs, which some sources bot-block; if a
source needs it, the fetch module routes through a commercial rendering proxy —
a config-level credential, not a per-scraper decision.

**Scanned archives are the open risk.** Material from the 1990s is often a
scan behind a PDF, which means OCR, which is the one stage with no obvious home
inside a Worker. It may force that stage — and only that stage — somewhere else.

## Ingestion

Everything between "bytes arrived" and "the corpus changed". It is one pipeline
whichever driver fed it, and **every stage is idempotent**, because the drivers
retry: a Workflow retries a step, and a cron pass re-runs whatever the last one
did not finish.

  fetched, without re-fetching them.

  request to somebody else's server, so a step that re-fetched on every retry would turn one
  flaky model call into a second full crawl of that slice — and the traffic most likely to
  get us blocked is the traffic we did not need to send.
  </details>

Walk an archive in slices, and make a retry cheap

Phase 7 of #34, over the same ingestion chain the cron uses — two drivers, one
pipeline, so a case that proved the backfill against different fakes would be
proving something else.

Two properties, both asserted rather than assumed. Slices are independent: a
slice reads and writes nothing another relies on, so one bad slice costs one
retry rather than a restart, which matters when decades of archive is thousands
of them. And a retried step does not re-fetch: the platform's retry re-runs a
whole step, every fetch inside one is a request to somebody else's server, and
what a previous attempt stored in R2 is what this one reads. The raw key is the
document's own key rather than a fetch time, because a timestamped key would
miss the stored payload on every retry.

Slices run oldest first. A backfill that starts at the recent end leaves the
corpus looking complete long before it is — a persona's page would show a thin
recent record with nothing saying the rest is still coming.

A document whose key carries no date belongs to no window. Guessing would put it
in one nobody established it was in, and windows are the whole shape of this.

The slice size stays an unchecked bet and says so: a year is the unit archives
are organised in, not a size anything says fits inside a Workflow's limits. It
is a named constant carrying that provenance, and the planner takes it as an
argument, so closing phase 1 is one call site rather than a rewrite.

input.head: claude/hitbut-backfill
input.body:
Phase 7 of #34 — the last phase that needs nothing from Cloudflare, built over the same ingestion chain the cron uses. Two drivers, one pipeline: a case proving the backfill against a different set of fakes would be proving something else. ## Two properties, both asserted **Slices are independent.** A slice reads and writes nothing another relies on, so one bad slice costs one retry rather than a restart. That matters because decades of archive is thousands of slices. `3.11` runs three years where the middle one's document is a dead URL, and holds the code to it: the failing slice reports rather than throws, its neighbours are untouched, and the corpus holds exactly the two that landed. **A retried step does not re-fetch.** The platform's retry re-runs the *whole* step, and every fetch inside one is a request to somebody else's server — so a step that re-fetched would turn one flaky model call into a second crawl of the slice. `3.12` rate-limits the stance model, watches all three documents get fetched and stored, then retries and asserts **zero** requests, three cache reads, nothing minted, and the stances the rate limit cost now recorded. The mechanism is one detail: the raw key is the document's own key, not a fetch time. A timestamped key would miss the stored payload on every retry — the no-re-fetch rule would silently not hold, and only a test that counts requests would ever notice. Both were seen failing first: forcing the cache read to `null` reddens `3.12` on "the retry issued no request"; dropping the window filter reddens `3.11`. ## Two judgement calls in the code **Oldest first.** A backfill that starts at the recent end leaves the corpus looking complete long before it is — a persona's page would show a thin recent record with nothing saying the rest is still coming, which is the same wrong implication `6.9`'s coverage statement exists to prevent, arriving from a different direction. **A key with no date belongs to no window.** Guessing would put a document in a window nobody established it was in, and windows are the whole shape of a backfill. `3.11` proves an undated key is not picked up even by a window spanning forty years. ## The slice size is a bet, and says so A year is the unit archives are organised in. It is **not** a size anything says fits inside a Workflow's step, duration and payload limits — the session that designed this could not reach Cloudflare's documentation to read them, which is #34's phase 1 and still open. So `SLICE_MONTHS` carries that provenance in its own comment rather than looking measured, and `plannedSlices` takes the size as an argument. Closing phase 1 is one call site, not a rewrite. ## Folders touched
**`src/backend/backfill/`** — new. `slice.ts` runs one window end to end and never throws for a document failure; `plan.ts` turns a date range into windows, oldest first, with the unverified size named as such. **`docs/architecture/`** — the backfill section gains the two properties, the ordering, and the honest note about the size.
## What this deliberately does not do **It is not wired to a Cloudflare Workflow.** `runSlice` is what a Workflow step would call, and the outcome it returns is what a step reads to decide on a retry — but the binding needs Workflows enabled on the account (#27), and the step/duration limits that decide the slice size need docs the sandbox cannot reach (#34 phase 1). What lands here is the part that can be proven against fixtures, which is what phase 7's exit condition asks for. ## Verification `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (62), `npm run test:server` (13, real workerd), `npm run test:screen` (14). `check_the_world.mjs`: 0 blocking. CI still cannot run — every workflow fails at startup, see #39. Refs #34 --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)_

input.commit_title: Walk an archive in slices, and make a retry cheap (#55)
input.commit_message:
Phase 7 of #34, over the same ingestion chain the cron uses. Slices are
independent, so one bad slice costs one retry rather than a restart; and a
retried step reads what the previous attempt stored in R2 rather than
re-fetching, because the platform re-runs a whole step and every fetch inside
one is a request to somebody else's server.

Slices run oldest first, and a document whose key carries no date belongs to no
window. The slice size stays an unchecked bet against Cloudflare's Workflow
limits and says so in its own name.

Merged without CI verification: GitHub Actions has been failing every run in
this repository at startup since 2026-08-22T00:01Z (see #39). Verified locally
instead — typecheck, 62 default-lane tests, 13 server on real workerd, 14 screen
goldens, and check_the_world at 0 blocking.

Refs #34
